t: Number of Subarrays With GCD Equal to K — GCD Extension
o: We count subarrays whose overall GCD is exactly k. Key fact: extending a subarray can only decrease (or keep) the GCD, and GCDs along fixed ends take O(log) distinct values. With n <= 1000, an O(n²) scan computing gcd incrementally is fine. In example 1 (nums=[9,3,1,2,6,3], k=3): subarrays [9,3], [3], [6,3], [3] (last element) have gcd 3 → 4 matches. Example 2: single element 4 never has gcd 7.
k: GCD of a growing subarray is non-increasing; once it drops below k (or loses divisibility by k) it can never return.
Incremental gcd: g = gcd(g, nums[j]) lets each extension be O(log).
Early break when g < k prunes most extensions in practice.

a.n: Approach 1: Fix Left End, Extend Right
a.i: For each start i, walk j from i rightward maintaining the running gcd; count whenever it equals k, and break as soon as the gcd becomes smaller than k (monotonicity means no later j can recover). Worst case O(n² log V), comfortably fast for n=1000. An optimization maps distinct gcd values per end with counts for O(n log V) behavior, but is unnecessary here.
s: For each i: g = 0; for j >= i: g = gcd(g, nums[j]).
If g == k, ans++; else if g < k, break inner loop.
a.t: O(n² log V) worst case — double loop with Euclidean gcd; fast in practice due to early breaks.

w: Remember gcd(0,x)=x seeds the running gcd correctly. Elements not divisible by k instantly kill the gcd below k — the break handles that. If n were 1e5, switch to the 'distinct gcds per right endpoint' technique: keep a map from gcd value to count of left endpoints, updated per step in O(log V) distinct entries. Watch that equality with k, not divisibility, is counted.
